Title: MRR‐Assisted MZI Crossbar Array for Energy‐Efficient Optical Parallel Computing
Text:
RESEARCH ARTICLE
www.lpr-journal.org
MRR-Assisted MZI Crossbar Array for Energy-Eﬃcient
Optical Parallel Computing
Shan Jiang, Xinyu Liu, Bo Wu, Shangsen Sun, Hailong Zhou, Jianji Dong,*
and Xinliang Zhang
Optical neural networks (ONNs) have emerged as a photonic platform for
accelerating artiﬁcial intelligence workloads, relying on optical matrix
operations as their computational basis. Yet existing implementations face
critical challenges in precision, cascaded optical loss, and ineﬃcient
weight-programming mechanisms, which limit scalability and practical
performance. A micro-ring resonator (MRR)-assisted Mach–Zehnder
interferometer (MZI) crossbar architecture (MMCA) that addresses these
limitations through parallelized optical computing is presented. By replacing
conventional waveguide-based coupling with MRR-enabled
wavelength-selective routing, the design suppresses the multiplicative optical
losses inherent in cascaded combiner networks. Concurrently, MZI-based
crossbar nodes enable deterministic one-to-one weight mapping with
enhanced speed and robustness. The architecture synergizes structural merits
from mainstream optical computing paradigms while overcoming critical
bottlenecks. Experimental validation demonstrates 6-bit weight-loading
precision and high energy eﬃciency. Integrated wavelength-division
multiplexing further enables parallel computation, achieving 95.1%
classiﬁcation accuracy on convolutional neural network benchmarks. This
approach establishes a scalable framework for low-loss, high-precision optical
matrix operations, advancing the development of energy-eﬃcient photonic AI
accelerators.
1. Introduction

intelligence, has grown central to advancing neural network
training and inference, where high-dimensional operations gov-
ern tasks ranging from image-processing convolutions,[1–3] and
recommendation-system matrix factorizations[4,5] to linguistic
embedding transformations.[6–8] Yet electronic von Neumann

In contrast, PCM arrays and analogous crossbar architec-

designs.[35,36] Nevertheless, the vertical branch waveguides use
2 × 1 directional couplers to combine light into the bus waveg-

system size. While parallel photodetectors could mitigate this

To resolve these competing constraints, we introduce an MRR-
assisted MZI crossbar parallel computing architecture (MMCA)
that synergizes precise MZI-based weight encoding with MRR-
mediated signal routing. This co-design eliminates coupling
losses except for ﬁxed fabrication-dependent MRR attenuation
(≈0.1 dB per device), achieving system-size-independent energy
eﬃciency. And this architecture leverages wavelength-division
multiplexing (WDM) to enable multi-wavelength parallel inputs.
Experimental validation through a 4 × 4 matrix core demon-
strates 6-bit weight precision and 95.1% accuracy in parallel con-
volutional neural network (CNN) classiﬁcation, which is com-
parable to that of an electronic computing system. The MMCA
achieved an energy eﬃciency of 21.7 pj/OP, highlighting its ef-
ﬁciency and potential for high-performance computing appli-
cations. The wavelength-parallelized inputs and loss-minimized
topology establish a scalable pathway for photonic computing
supremacy.

Figure 1b. The operating wavelength of the input signals is de-
termined by the resonance conditions of the MRRs. Figure 1c
illustrates the resonance characteristics of the MRRs. Since all
MRRs are fabricated with identical design parameters, they ex-
hibit the same extinction ratio, free spectral range (FSR), and
quality factor (Q-factor). To ensure uniformity, all MRRs in the
same row are tuned to an identical resonant wavelength. The
resonant wavelengths of MRRs in diﬀerent rows are evenly dis-
tributed within one FSR. It is important to highlight two key
design considerations for the MRRs: 1) Since the primary func-
tion of the MRRs is to route light at their resonant wavelengths,
their Q-factor must not be excessively high, as an overly high
Q-factor would make them highly sensitive to fabrication im-
perfections and environmental ﬂuctuations, leading to unstable
output optical intensity. 2) Conversely, the Q-factor should not
be too low, as this would result in excessive optical coupling
from the bus waveguide into the branches, thereby causing signal
crosstalk.
Once the resonant states of the MRRs are tuned, the oper-
ating wavelength for each row is determined. When multiple
sets of wavelengths with a spacing of an integer multiple of
FSRs are used as inputs, the dimensionality of the input vec-
tors is expanded, transforming matrix–vector multiplication into
matrix–matrix multiplication. For an M×N MMCA system with
K sets of wavelength channels, the optical signals X1k to XMk,
corresponding to the kth column of the input matrix X, as de-

with wavelengths spaced by n (n = 1, 2, 3…) FSRs are com-

MMCA core used in our experiment, as shown in Figure 1d,
two sets of wavelengths 𝜆1∼4 and 𝜆5∼8 are selected, correspond-
ing to eight laser source channels, to construct a 4 × 2 matrix
input.
The MZIs function as tunable weight elements of W. The opti-
cal intensity output from the lower port of each MZI corresponds
to the result of the numerical multiplication Wmn×Xmk, and the
residual optical power exits the upper port and propagates to the
subsequent cascaded MZI. The lower port of MZI also serves as
the Add port of the MRR. As the input wavelengths match the
resonance frequency of the MRR, the signals are coupled into
the MRR and subsequently coupled into its drop port. The drop
ports of a column of MRRs share a common bus waveguide, so
the optical signals output from the DROP ports are inherently
summed within this waveguide. It mitigates the multiplication of
coupling loss typically introduced during traditional beam com-
bining. The output Y, representing the parallel matrix multipli-
cation results, is separated by a wavelength demultiplexer (DE-
MUX) with wavelength spacing of an FSR and then detected by
photodetectors.

the MZIs serve as tunable weight elements. For an MZI, the re-
sulting optical intensities at the two output ports are mutually

In practice, minor coupling loss occurs in the directional cou-
plers, along with small propagation loss in crossing waveguides.
To compensate for these errors, we pre-characterize the loss
and apply the corresponding correction factors to the matrix
mapped onto the MMCA. Details of the compensation method
are provided in Section S2 (Supporting Information). Thanks to
the crossbar architecture, weights can be conﬁgured row-by-row.
Once the weight assignment for all rows is completed, the verti-
cal intensity ratios between rows can be measured, and the input
matrix can then be scaled by a coeﬃcient corresponding to these
ratios to achieve vertical weight adjustment. It enables rapid one-
to-one mapping for MZI weight assignment without algorith-
mic assistance. Once tuned to their designated resonant states,
the MRRs remain ﬁxed without requiring further voltage adjust-
ments, avoiding the instability and low precision that are often
associated with weight loading in MRR-based architectures.
The chip is fabricated on a standard 220 nm silicon-on-
insulator wafer, with single-mode waveguides 500 nm in width.
A microscope image of the fabricated chip is shown in Figure
2a. The chip occupies a footprint of 2.5 × 1.9 mm2. Thermo-
optic phase shifters made of TiN heaters, deposited on the silica
cladding, are used to modulate the eﬀective refractive index dis-
tribution of the MZIs and MRRs. Deep trenches surrounding the
MZIs and MRRs act as thermal isolators and, together with a ther-
moelectric cooler (TEC), maintain stable thermal conditions dur-
ing operation. Figure 2b presents the structure of an MRR, which
features a radius of 20 μm, a coupling gap of 0.18 μm, and a bent
waveguide angle of 70°. The performance of the MRR was ﬁrst
evaluated by measuring its transmission spectrum. As shown in
Figure 2c, the FSR in the C-band is ≈4.54 nm, and the insertion
loss is ≈0.1 dB.
We input light at wavelengths of 1552.565, 1553.7, 1554.835,
and 1555.97 nm, and sweep the voltage applied to the TiN heater
to tune the state of the MRR. The transmission curves are pre-
sented in Figure 2d, where the measured inter-channel crosstalk
is less than −18 dB. Figure 2e shows the normalized output inten-
sity from one arm of the MZI as the voltage applied to the thermal
phase shifter is varied, and the power consumption for achieving
a 𝜋-phase shift is 25.1 mW. In Figure 2f, the chip is shown inte-
grated within a robust optical and electrical packaging module.
(see Section S3, Supporting Information, for characterization de-

Next, we demonstrate the applicability of the proposed archi-
tecture in a CNN task. Figure 4a illustrates the architecture of the
CNN employed in our experiment. Two images are encoded us-
ing two distinct sets of wavelengths, respectively. The ﬁrst layer is
a convolutional layer comprising four 2 × 2 kernels. Each kernel
is ﬂattened into a 4 × 1 vector and mapped onto a separate col-
umn of the MMCA core. As a result, the encoded signals of the
two input images can be simultaneously convolved with all four
kernels, enabling parallel execution of multiple convolution op-
erations. The output feature maps are individually ﬂattened into
a 2916 × 1 vector in the computer, activated by ReLU, and sub-
sequently fed into a fully connected layer, which outputs to a 10-
neuron classiﬁcation layer activated by SoftMax.
Since the proposed architecture supports only non-negative-
valued multiplications, each convolutional kernel is decomposed
into its positive and negative components during inference.
These components are processed separately, and the ﬁnal result
is obtained by subtracting the negative contribution from the pos-
itive one. Figure 4b shows the confusion matrix corresponding
to the classiﬁcation results obtained from testing 1000 images.
The proposed system achieves an accuracy of 95.1%, which is
comparable to the 96.4% accuracy achieved using a conventional
64-bit digital computer. The slightly reduced accuracy of the op-
toelectronic computing system is primarily attributed to the lim-
ited modulation resolution of the VOAs and minor fabrication
imperfections.
3. Discussion and Conclusion
As a distinctive alternative to conventional matrix multiplication
architectures, the MMCA architecture innovatively integrates the
advantages of three mainstream computational paradigms while
eﬀectively mitigating their respective drawbacks. The proposed
architecture exhibits the following key advantages:
1) Reduced optical loss. In conventional crossbar-based architec-
tures, to ensure uniform output power across rows, they re-
quire specially designed coupling coeﬃcients, causing a sig-
niﬁcant portion of the signal in each vertical bus segment to
be coupled out and lost. This loss accumulates and increases
with network size. For an M × N structure, optical combining
introduces at least 10 × lg(1/M) dB of loss. In contrast, our
design replaces waveguide-based couplers with MRRs. When
the optical signal couples from the MRR into the bus waveg-
uide, it introduces an insertion loss of ≈0.1 dB (Figure 5).
As the signal propagates along the bus waveguide and passes
through other MRRs that are at diﬀerent-resonance, only neg-
ligible crosstalk (<−18 dB) is observed, and can therefore be
safely ignored. Thus, the signal propagating in the vertical
bus of our architecture does not experience cascaded losses.

2) Enhanced weight-loading precision. The weight-loading com-

that of the MRR, the required DAC precision can be sub-

Information).
3) Fast weight assignment. The cascaded MZI design struc-
ture enables explicit weight loading by directly calculating the
splitting ratios of MZIs to determine the required voltages.
This process bypasses the need for training, thereby reducing
time and computational overhead, making it especially suit-
able for applications requiring frequent matrix reconﬁgura-
tion.

To further enhance the performance of the MMCA architec-
ture, several potential directions can be considered. 1) Although
MRRs require only minimal power to maintain their resonance
states during operation, the overall energy consumption can be
further reduced by integrating PCM.[37] By replacing thermal
phase shifters with PCM, energy is required only during state
transitions, thereby eliminating static power consumption dur-
ing steady-state operation. 2) Indeed, the consistency of MRRs is
a critical factor that currently limits the number of parallel input
data sets. In our present design, the primary role of the MRRs
is optical ﬁltering. To improve fabrication tolerance, this ﬁltering
functionality could be achieved using alternative structures with
broader and more tolerant spectral responses,[38] thereby relaxing
the requirement for strict resonance alignment. 3) Besides, the
increase in parallelism in the experiment imposes a signiﬁcant
demand on wavelength resources. Therefore, an arrayed waveg-
uide grating can be employed to replace MRRs in a column. With
only four wavelengths, the arrayed waveguide grating (AWG) en-
ables the input of four groups of parallel signals, and our archi-
tecture would require sixteen wavelength channels. By replacing
both the MRRs and the DEMUX, the AWG signiﬁcantly reduces
the number of components and enhances wavelength utilization
eﬃciency.[39] Detailed information can be found in Section S6
(Supporting Information). Moreover, compared to MRRs, passive
components such as AWGs exhibit greater thermal insensitivity.
This opens up future possibilities for enhanced thermal stability
and accuracy.
Overall, this work oﬀers a new architectural paradigm for ten-
sor computation in photonic neural network accelerators and
demonstrates signiﬁcant potential for advancing energy-eﬃcient
AI hardware.
